title: The Personalization of Conversational Agents in Health Care: Systematic Review
extended_summary:
This paper systematically reviews how personalization has been implemented in health care conversational agents. The authors were interested in understanding what kinds of personalization have been used, for whom they were targeted, how the personalization was automated, and how these features were evaluated. The review is framed around conversational agents with unconstrained natural language input, including chatbots and embodied conversational agents.

Across 13 included studies, personalization most commonly affected the content of dialogue, such as tailored feedback, reminders, warnings, alerts, and recommendations. A smaller number of studies adapted conversational style or the user interface, and a few used either explicit user input, implicit sensing from interaction history or audiovisual cues, or a combination of both to drive adaptation. The reviewed systems were used for mental health support, mindfulness coaching, asthma self-management, diabetes monitoring, pain reporting, exercise and sun protection promotion, and reflection on physical activity.

The review concludes that personalization in health care conversational agents was limited and generally not evidence-based. Most studies did not use explicit theoretical frameworks for personalization and rarely evaluated personalization itself as a distinct factor. Only a few studies directly assessed personalized features, and the authors argue that future research should more carefully examine how personalization affects user engagement, health outcomes, privacy, safety, and decision-making.

identified_tools.name: CAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Conversational artificial intelligence system: an interactive natural-language dialogue agent that can deliver personalized content, feedback, reminders, and adaptive conversational responses.
identified_tools.use_case: Systematic review of 13 health-care conversational agents with unconstrained natural-language input, focusing on how personalization was implemented and evaluated across studies rather than on a single named product.

findings.finding_summary: Across 13 included studies, personalization was commonly implemented for tailored content, but the review reports that it was usually not supported by a theoretical framework and was only directly evaluated in 2 studies. The authors conclude that personalization features were associated in the reviewed literature with higher user satisfaction, engagement, and dialogue quality, but the role of personalization in improving health outcomes was not directly assessed.
findings.measure: User satisfaction, user engagement, dialogue quality, and reported health outcomes across included studies

quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review, so the evidence is synthesized rather than a single controlled evaluation. However, the paper explicitly notes limited direct assessment of personalization and little ability to attribute outcomes to the personalization features themselves.
impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests potential benefits for satisfaction, engagement, and dialogue quality, but it does not provide pooled effect sizes or direct evidence of impact on outcomes. The overall impact is therefore promising but unclear.
